title: Chapter 12 – Red Snow
html:
The talismans need blood.

Not much. A few drops of dried first-rank beast blood in each pot of ink, ground fine and stirred in with the cinnabar and the soot, to give the lines something living to hold the Qi. It is the oldest part of the recipe, older than the Lin family, and no one knows why it works. It simply does. Without it, a talisman is only a pretty drawing.

By the last weeks of winter, the household's store of it is gone.

"Enough for forty," says Father at the council, holding up a small clay jar. "Perhaps fifty, if I'm careful. The Sect wants two hundred in twenty days."

Silence around the table. No one has hunted past the stream line since the wolf.

"The Salt Hollow," says Fourth Uncle at last.

Everyone knows it. A hollow on the north stream, two hours' walk up the old deer trail, where mineral springs bubble up through the rocks and leave the stones crusted white with salt. In winter the deer and the boars and the mist rabbits come down from the hills to lick the salt, and a good hunter can take a season's worth of first-rank blood there in two days. It is inside the stream line. Only just.

"Not you," says Grandfather to Fourth Uncle. "Not with the gate as it is. And not your guards. Farmers with mantle bracers are no use against what drained that wolf." He looks around the table. "Lin Mao will lead. He knows the trail. Feng with him. And two of the cousins."

"Lin Bo," says Third Aunt at once. "He's at the fourth layer. He's good with snares, and he can bind a boar with the Green Pulse long enough for the others to reach it." She says it proudly. Her only son.

"And Lin Shu," says Uncle Mao. "He needs the experience. Two days, out and back. Daylight only. We'll camp in the old charcoal burners' hut by the springs. If we see anything we don't like, we come home."

Grandfather nods slowly. "Two days."

Second Uncle writes it down. The trail. The day. The hour of leaving. The names. Lin Jian, behind the screen, watches the silver pencil move across the page, and feels something cold settle in his stomach that has nothing to do with the winter.

\ \ \*

That night he goes to his father's desk.

His father is drawing, as always, by lamplight, the left hand braced against the right. He glances up when his son comes in and sits down on the floor beside him, and goes back to his work without a word. They have been doing this for months: the boy sitting, the man drawing, and every now and then the boy saying something like the ink goes fat there, and the man adjusting a stroke.

Tonight Lin Jian sets a small, stoppered clay bottle on the desk.

"What's that?"

"Pepper," says Lin Jian. "From Old Hu's bath. The red bark. I boiled it down." He has not boiled it down. He has spent three nights separating the oil out of a pot of the bark sludge left over from the tempering decoction, a few tenths of a point of Qi at a time, until he had a thimbleful of something so strong that the cork alone makes his eyes stream.

```
[Separation: Capsaicinoid Concentrate]
Source: red-pepper bark residue
Purity: 91%
Note: Extreme mucosal irritant. Aerosol exposure incapacitating.
```

His father uncorks it, sniffs, and recoils so hard he nearly falls off his stool. His eyes fill. He coughs for a full minute.

"Gods," he says. "What do you want with this?"

"Can you put it in a Flame-Burst?" says Lin Jian. "In the paper. Soak the paper in it before you draw. So when it bursts, it's not just fire. It's smoke. Pepper smoke."

His father stares at him with streaming eyes.

"For Feng," says Lin Jian. "For the hunt."

For a long moment his father says nothing at all. Then he wipes his eyes on his sleeve, very carefully corks the bottle, and takes three fresh sheets of the new paper from the stack.

He draws three of them that night. It takes him until the small hours. He has to stop twice to go outside and breathe. The finished talismans are a faint, angry orange instead of yellow, and they smell, even dry, like a fire in a spice market.

In the morning, Lin Jian finds his brother in the gate yard, checking the straps of his pack.

"Here," he says, and holds them out.

Lin Feng takes them, sniffs, and jerks his head back. "What are these?"

"Flame-Bursts. Father made them. There's pepper in the paper." He hesitates. "If something comes for you, don't throw it at its body. Throw it at its face."

His brother looks at the three orange slips in his hand, and then at Lin Jian, and for a moment something moves behind his eyes. Then he snorts.

"Go back to bed, radish."

But he tucks the talismans into the front of his short robe, where he can reach them, and buttons the short robe over them, and does not take them out again.

\ \ \*

The night before they leave, in the dry quarry behind the terraces, Lin Jian tests the paper.

He has done this every night this week, in the gap between the second watch and the third, when the night guards are looking outward and Old Hu's sleeping tonic has put the household's two light sleepers under. Tonight he has a straw dummy bound to a post, a bucket of water, and the fourth of Father's pepper talismans, the one that came out too faint to trust.

He starts with feet. Cloudstep first, the way Old Hu taught it: the breath drawn down into the heel, the Qi thrown out through the sole like a spring uncoiling. The loose gravel does not crunch. He crosses the quarry in six strides, turns on a toe, and crosses back in five, and the fifth is clean, and he stores the feeling away for the next time.

Then hands. He pinches the talisman between two fingers, pushes a thread of Qi into the corner node, and flicks it at the dummy's face from nine paces. It bursts a hand's breadth short, in the air, and an orange cloud rolls out over the straw.

The cloud is the problem. It drifts back toward him on the breeze.

He steps through it in his mind, the way he steps through a failed print: wrong release point, wrong wind. He tries again with the next test slip, and this time he throws low and slightly to the left, so the burst lands upwind of the dummy and the smoke rolls away from him. Then, before the cloud thins, he sets his palm to the ground and raises the Earthen Rampart, a knee-high shoulder of packed stone between himself and the haze, and drops behind it, and counts to twelve.

Nothing reaches him. When he rises, the dummy's straw face is blackened and the bucket beside it has a rind of red grit on the water.

Throw, shield, wait. Three beats. It is not a technique. It is a habit, and he runs it nine more times, until his Qi is a thin warm thread and his hands shake, and then he sits down in the gravel and breathes.

```
[Practice Log: Combination — Burst / Rampart / Cloudstep]
Qi efficiency: 78% → 91% over 10 repetitions
Note: Response time under 2 seconds recommended.
```

Two seconds. A man in a feather cloak, or whatever he is, will not give him two seconds. But Feng might get one.

\ \ \*

They leave at first light: Uncle Mao limping in front with his cane and his short sword, Lin Feng behind with his spear, Lin Bo cheerful and red-cheeked with a coil of snare wire over his shoulder, Lin Shu thin and quiet at the back. Third Aunt walks with them to the gate and straightens her son's collar and tells him to keep his feet dry. Lin Bo laughs and kisses her cheek, and runs to catch up.

Lin Jian watches from the eastern wall until they disappear into the trees on the north slope.

Then he stays there.

He spends the whole of that day on the wall. He tells Old Hu he is ill, which Old Hu does not believe, and Old Hu lets him go anyway. He sits with his back to a merlon and his knees drawn up and lets his sense go out as far as it will reach, which is not far. The walls. The terraces. The edge of the trees. He cannot feel the hunters. They are beyond him, two hours up a trail he has never walked.

He feels other things.

The birds, mostly. The bright, tiny sparks of crows and jays in the trees below. And as the afternoon goes on he notices that the sparks are moving. Not scattering the way birds scatter in the evening. Gathering. Drifting, in twos and threes, to the northeast, until in the last of the light he can see them with his eyes as well, a slow black wheel in the gray sky over the north slope, turning and turning.

Crows circle over something that is dead, or about to be.

He goes to his grandfather. He tells him about the birds.

The old man looks north for a long time, his face unreadable. Then he says, "They're camped by the springs tonight. If they're not home by noon tomorrow, we go and look." And he goes on looking north until the light is gone.

\ \ \*

Old Hu is waiting at the north gate when Lin Jian comes back from the wall, sitting on an upturned bucket with his iron rod across his knees.

"Blood arts," says the old man, without looking round. "You were thinking it."

"I was thinking about the wolf."

"Same thing." Hu rubs his bad shoulder. "Listen, because I'll say this once. Everyone worth killing in this world has a ladder. Body, Qi, soul. The body is flesh and bone and blood. Temper it and you can take a blow. The Qi is what you push through the body, and it is what the Sect teaches, and it is what your uncle Mao has been tempering for forty years. The soul is a third thing. Spiritual sense is the first sign of it. Your father has a little. You have more than you should."

Lin Jian keeps his face still.

"Blood arts steal from the second to feed the first. They drink another man's Qi through his blood and make it theirs. It is fast, and it is filthy, and it rots the soul from the inside, so the ones who walk it end up as that wolf. Thin and hungry and never full." Hu spits in the snow. "Whoever your man in the feathers is, he has walked it a long way. Which means he is stronger than he looks and stupider than he thinks. A man who feeds on Qi cannot feed on pepper."

"I know."

"I know you know. Your brother told me what the paper did." The old teacher turns his head at last and his gaze is steady. "Now tell me what happens when the pepper wears off."

Lin Jian thinks about it. "He's angry."

"He's angry, and he's hungry, and the hunters are in a hollow with one way out." Hu stands, with the rod, and his knees crack. "Pray your uncle knows how to count. And pray the paper is enough, because a thing like that does not stay blind for long, and it will remember who blinded it."

He walks away toward the forge, rod tapping on the frozen ground, and does not say anything else. Lin Jian stands at the gate until the cold works through his boots, looking at the trail, and the crows that have not come yet.

\ \ \*

Lin Shu comes home in the middle of the night.

The guards on the gate hear him before they see him: a high, thin, broken sound coming up the north trail, like an animal in a trap. Then a shape comes stumbling out of the trees into the moonlight, falling, getting up, falling again. A boy with no cloak and no boots, his feet bloody, one arm hanging, his face a mask of tears and snot and terror.

By the time Lin Jian gets to the gate, half the household is there, and Third Aunt is on her knees in the snow holding Lin Shu by the shoulders and shaking him, and he is trying to talk and cannot.

On his forearm, through the torn sleeve, there is a burn. Small and round, the size of a thumbprint.

"He was waiting," Lin Shu says at last. His voice is a croak. "At the Hollow. When we got there. He was just sitting on a rock by the spring. Waiting for us." His teeth chatter so hard he can barely get the words out. "A man. In a cloak. Made of feathers. And when he moved, there was mist. Red mist."

Third Aunt's hands go very still on his shoulders.

"Bo," she says. "Where is Bo?"

Lin Shu looks at her. And then he looks away, and begins to cry again, and does not answer, and that is the answer.

Third Aunt makes a sound Lin Jian will remember for the rest of his life.

\ \ \*

The story comes out in pieces, between the sobbing, while Grandfather stands over the boy like a statue.

The man in the feather cloak had gone for Lin Bo first. Not because Bo was the strongest. Because Bo was nearest. He had simply stepped out of the red mist beside him, and put two fingers to his throat, and Lin Bo had gone white and folded up in the snow like an empty cloak, and the mist around them had turned pink.

Then the man had turned to Lin Feng.

"He wanted Feng," Lin Shu says. "He looked at all of us and then he looked at Feng and he smiled. Like he was hungry. Like Feng was something to eat."

Uncle Mao had thrown up a wall of earth between them, and a storm of stone shards from the hollow's floor, and the man in the feathers had walked through both of them as if they were rain. Then Lin Feng had pulled something orange out of his short robe and thrown it straight at the man's face and screamed burst.

"It went off like," Lin Shu chokes, "like a fire full of chilies. And the man screamed. He screamed and clawed at his eyes, and the mist went everywhere." He wipes his nose on his sleeve. "And Feng threw the second one. And Uncle Mao picked Feng up, he just picked him up, like a sack, Feng was hurt, his leg, the man had touched his leg, and Uncle Mao threw me. Off the edge of the hollow. Down the slope toward home. He said run. He said run and tell the Patriarch. So I ran." His voice breaks. "I ran. I left them. I ran."

"You did right," says Grandfather. His voice is very quiet and very steady. "Where were they, when you ran?"

"In the hollow. Uncle Mao was carrying Feng toward the rocks. The man was still screaming." He looks up, his face wrecked. "But he was getting up."

\ \ \*

Grandfather goes himself.

Lin Jian has never seen it before. In seven years, he has never once seen his grandfather put on the old sword: a long, plain blade in a cracked black leather scabbard that hangs on the wall of the main hall above the Patriarch's chair, notched along its edge, reground so many times that it is thinner than it ought to be. It belonged to Lin Shoucheng. Grandfather takes it down from the wall and buckles it on over his robe with steady hands, and the household goes silent.

Old Hu comes out of the granary with the leather case under his arm and the iron rod in his hand. No one asked him to. He simply comes, and stands by the gate, and waits.

Su Qinghe is already there, in her gray hunting robe, with her knife across the small of her back and her hair bound tight. She does not ask whether she can go. Grandfather does not tell her she cannot.

"Wenyuan," Grandfather says. "Wenshi. You hold the hill. Every guard on the walls. Every child in the main hall. If we are not back by dawn," he pauses, "you will know what to do."

Fourth Uncle nods, white-faced. Father says nothing. He looks at his wife.

She looks back at him for a moment. Then she turns and goes out of the gate, and Grandfather and Old Hu go with her, and the three of them move up the north trail into the dark faster than Lin Jian has ever seen anyone move, Grandfather's white hair a pale blur among the trees, until they are gone.

Third Aunt is standing in the gate yard in the snow with no cloak on. Nobody can make her come inside. In the end Lin Jian goes and stands beside her, and after a while she puts her hand on his shoulder, and grips it so hard it hurts, and he does not move.

\ \ \*

They come back at dawn.

The guards see the lights first. Then the shapes. Grandfather walking in front, his robe torn and his sword drawn, and behind him something floating a foot above the snow on a cushion of green Qi that streams from the old man's left hand: a litter of cut pine branches, and on it, Lin Feng. Pale as the snow. Breathing.

Then Old Hu, with Uncle Mao's arm over his one shoulder, the old teacher's leg dragging, wrapped in bloody cloth to the hip.

Then Su Qinghe.

She is carrying Lin Bo.

She carries him the way you carry a sleeping child, his head on her shoulder, his arms hanging. He is very light. Even from the wall, Lin Jian can see how light he is. Like a cloak on a hook.

Third Aunt does not scream this time. She walks out of the gate and down the road to meet them, and Su Qinghe stops, and Third Aunt takes her son out of her arms and sits down in the snow in the middle of the road with him in her lap, and holds him, and rocks, and makes no sound at all.

Nobody goes near her for a long time.

\ \ \*

Lin Feng is laid on a pallet in the main hall, by the brazier. His left leg, below the knee, is a horror: the flesh around a round, thumb-sized burn gone gray and puckered and cold to the touch, and the gray spreading upward toward the knee in thin, branching lines, like frost on a window.

"Blood Qi," says Old Hu. He kneels beside the pallet with his face like stone. "It touched him. Put some of itself into him. If it reaches the heart," he does not finish.

The household healer, an elderly side-branch aunt with a bag of herbs and the Ward Art, works on him for an hour. The gray lines do not stop. They creep upward, a hair's breadth at a time.

Lin Jian sits by his brother's head and does what he has never once done in front of witnesses. He puts his hand on Lin Feng's forehead, as if feeling for fever, and scans.

```
[Scan: Lin Feng]
Root: wood / fire / earth — intact
Blood volume: 58%
Foreign energy: blood-attribute Qi, active, spreading (left leg → thigh)
Structure: 71% similarity to residue in Hu Tieshou (shared cultivation lineage)
Prognosis: survival likely if foreign energy is expelled within 3 days
Separation from living tissue: LOCKED (Level 3+)
```

Seventy-one percent the same as the thing in Old Hu's shoulder. Not the same man. The same teacher. The same art.

And locked. He cannot touch living tissue. Not at Level Two.

He sits there with his hand on his brother's forehead and makes himself think, the way he always makes himself think, when everything in him wants to scream.

He cannot separate the poison out of Lin Feng. But he can separate it out of anything that is not Lin Feng.

"Aunt," he says, to the side-branch healer. "The blood-stop poultice. The one Third Aunt makes, with the willow. Does it draw things out of a wound?"

The old woman looks at him, surprised. "Some. It draws the heat. Why?"

"Can we put one on? And change it often? Very often?"

She shrugs, and makes one, and packs it around the gray wound, and binds it.

When she goes to fetch more water, Lin Jian lays his hand on the poultice.

The poultice is not Lin Feng. It is willow bark and blood-stop grass and a little of the gray poison that has crept out of the wound into it. The interface sees all three, layered, separate.

```
[Separation: Poultice (Contaminated)]
Target: blood-attribute Qi residue
Required Qi: 0.22
```

It costs very little. He does it, and feels the cold gray thread pulled out of the poultice and burned off into nothing, and the poultice is clean again, and hungry, and draws a little more out of the wound.

He does it again. And again.

He does it every few minutes, all night, sitting by his brother's head with his hand resting on the poultice as if he is simply holding it in place. Old Hu sits on the other side of the pallet and watches him do it and says nothing at all. At some point in the small hours, Third Aunt comes in out of the snow, finally, with her face like ash, and stands at the foot of the pallet, and sees what he is doing, and does not understand it, and kneels down and puts her own two green-glowing hands on her nephew's leg beside his and pours the Green Pulse into it, binding the flesh, holding it, while the tears run down her face.

The gray lines stop at the knee. Then, near dawn, they begin very slowly to go back.

Lin Jian's Qi runs out an hour before sunrise. He keeps his hand where it is anyway.

\ \ \*

Lin Feng wakes up in the morning.

He looks at the ceiling for a while. Then he turns his head, and sees his brother sitting beside him with gray circles under his eyes, and his hand on the poultice.

"Radish," he says. His voice is a thread. "It worked."

"What did?"

"The pepper." Lin Feng's mouth twitches. "Right in his face. He screamed like a pig." His eyes close. "One of his eyes went white. I saw it. Before Uncle Mao picked me up."

Lin Jian finds that he cannot say anything at all. He puts his other hand over his brother's, on the blanket, and Lin Feng turns his hand over and holds on.

They stay like that for a long time.

Then Lin Feng opens his eyes again, and they are clear and hard and awake.

"Only the council knew," he says, very quietly. "The trail. The day. The hour. Who was going." He looks at his brother. "He was waiting for us. Somebody told him."

Lin Jian looks at him, and nods.

Across the hall, by the door, Second Uncle is standing with his hands folded in his sleeves, watching the family gathered round the pallet. His face, for once, holds no expression at all. Then he turns, and looks for a long moment at the doors, and at the dark beyond them, as if he is listening for something out there in the snow.
